analysis.one_liner: Lets states take over environmental review of federal grazing allotments at a governor's request.
analysis.headline: The bill was never acted on after its referral to committee and died with no cosponsors at the end of the 114th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the federal law governing public lands so that, at a governor's request, the Interior Department must sign a 20-year agreement letting a state manage grazing allotments on federal land. The state would take over the federal government's job of deciding whether grazing-related projects — vegetation clearing, pinyon-juniper removal, and changes in how many cattle are permitted — need environmental review, and it could declare them exempt from review altogether. Disputes would go to a state-created process instead of the federal land appeals board. Each state could manage only two allotments, but the Interior Secretary could waive that limit entirely.
analysis.who_benefits: Ranchers holding Bureau of Land Management grazing permits. Under state management, the party issuing their permits and reviewing their grazing levels would no longer be a neutral federal agency but a state government whose officials are far closer to the livestock industry, and decisions could bypass federal environmental review. Governors asking for the agreements would also gain authority over federal land inside their borders.

how_it_helps.text: A state managing an allotment would inherit the federal government's responsibilities under the National Environmental Policy Act, including deciding whether vegetation projects, pinyon-juniper treatments, and changes in permitted cattle numbers qualify for categorical exclusion from environmental review [S2] [S3].
The agreements would run for 20 years, renewable for another 20, giving permit holders long-term state-level management rather than federal oversight [S3].

Disputes over state decisions would be resolved through a process developed by the state itself, and the bill expressly removes the Interior Board of Land Appeals' authority to hear such cases, eliminating the existing independent federal appeal route [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public that owns the federal land. Americans would lose independent federal environmental review and the right to appeal grazing decisions to the federal land appeals board on allotments turned over to state management. Federal land would be managed to the benefit of private permit holders with weaker checks, while taxpayers continue to fund the program.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public that owns federal land

drawbacks.text: The bill strips appeals from the Interior Board of Land Appeals for state-managed allotments and substitutes a dispute process the state itself designs, so the state would referee its own decisions [S3].

Although each state could initially manage only two allotments, the Interior Secretary could waive that cap without any statutory limit, so the small pilot framing could expand to any number of allotments at an administration's discretion [S3].

Moving environmental-review decisions to state governments closely tied to grazing interests would weaken the federal check on livestock impacts on public land, which conservation groups and the public traditionally rely on [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ranchers, state control promises faster vegetation treatments and grazing decisions and a friendlier referee. For the public, the cost is real: independent federal review and appeal rights on public land would be handed to a state process the state writes itself, with a waivable cap that could let the arrangement spread. The public's ownership stake in the land gets the weaker end of the trade.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its Federal Lands Subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and not a single cosponsor.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Stewart (R-UT) introduced the bill on April 14, 2015, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources [S1] [S5].
On June 5, 2015, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Federal Lands, the last action ever taken on it [S5].
No member joined as a cosponsor during the entire two-year Congress [S4].
The bill never received a subcommittee markup, committee vote, or floor vote before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, federal environmental review and the independent federal appeals process remain in place for BLM grazing allotments. The general public that owns the land is better off; the ranching interests and governors who would have gained authority over allotments are not.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public keeping federal grazing oversight

for.name: Rep. Chris Stewart
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to committee; no further action he took appears in the record.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chair never scheduled a markup)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 14, 2015, sent it to the Federal Lands Subcommittee on June 5, 2015, and never reported the bill out.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern beyond the Republican sponsor's identity appears in the record.

industries.industry: Federal grazing permit holders (Western livestock ranchers)
industries.note: State management would put permit decisions, cattle-number determinations, and vegetation-clearing approvals in the hands of governments close to the industry, replacing review by a neutral federal agency, and would remove the independent federal appeal board. The industry's gain comes directly out of the public's oversight of land the public owns.

industries.industry: Environmental and conservation interests, and public-lands oversight itself
industries.note: Federal NEPA review and IBLA appeals — the public's main levers over grazing on federal land — would be displaced on state-managed allotments. Their loss is the public's loss of a check on how shared land is used.
